claims.text: The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy has dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries.
Internal boundaries in the unmodified alloy are prone to microcrack initiation during tensile loading.
Approximately 0.5 at.% Nb should be added to the eutectic high-entropy alloy.
Rapid solidification will preserve the lamellar-colony structure.
Annealing at approximately 800°C for 1 hour will enable Nb diffusion and targeted precipitate formation.
An immediate rapid quench after annealing will prevent precipitate overaging and coarsening.
The intervention will form coherent nanoscale Nb-rich precipitates at internal lamellar-colony boundaries.
Nb atoms will segregate to internal boundaries during annealing.
Boundary segregation of Nb will facilitate nucleation of finely dispersed precipitates.
The Nb-rich precipitates will enhance internal-boundary cohesion.
The Nb-rich precipitates will obstruct dislocation motion and improve work hardening.
The Nb-rich precipitates will impede microcrack nucleation and propagation.
The Nb-modified alloy will have higher tensile strength than the identically processed Nb-free control.
The Nb-modified alloy will have higher room-temperature uniform elongation than the identically processed Nb-free control.
The Nb-modified alloy will have higher fracture toughness than the identically processed Nb-free control.
The unmodified alloy's weak internal boundaries cause premature microcrack formation and limited ductility.
The beneficial effects depend on controlling Nb content, annealing temperature, annealing duration, and quenching.
Deviations from the specified processing window may cause precipitate coarsening and embrittlement.
Analogous alloy systems support a mechanism involving precipitate strengthening together with enhanced ductility.
